notice: MODEL and CHEAP come from src/data/facts.json. Model IDs drift, so lab 00 prints the live list for you to check against.
text_of joins every text block. Every lab uses it instead of content[0].text, because on current models the first block is often a thinking block.
About 6,000 tokens clears every current minimum, including Haiku 4.5's 4,096. Your count will differ slightly by model, because current models use a newer tokenizer.
Below the model's minimum, caching fails silently: no error, just cache_creation_input_tokens of 0. Measuring the prefix is the only way to know.
write is the whole prefix up to and including the block that carries cache_control: both system blocks. You paid 1.25x base input on those tokens.
uncached_in is only the question after the breakpoint. That split is what makes caching cheap when the prefix is large and the suffix is small.

c07.output:
run 2
  write=0       read=6031    uncached_in=13
run 3
  write=0       read=6031    uncached_in=11
notice: write drops to 0 and read equals the earlier write: the second and third calls reused the stored prefix at 0.1x input price.
The questions changed but sit after the breakpoint, so they do not affect the cache key. Only content before the breakpoint has to match byte for byte.
Each read also refreshes the 5-minute TTL, so steady traffic keeps the entry warm without a longer TTL.

c09.output:
poisoned run 1
  write=6046    read=0       uncached_in=12
poisoned run 2
  write=6046    read=0       uncached_in=10

read stays at 0. Every call is now a fresh write at 1.25x input price.
The fix is PLACEMENT, not TTL: move volatile values out of the cached prefix.
notice: Nothing errored. The only signal is cache_read_input_tokens falling to 0 while cache_creation_input_tokens stays high on every call.
A longer TTL would not help, because the prefix never repeats. The fix is to move the timestamp after the breakpoint (for example, into the user message).
In a typical failure scenario like this one, the deciding clue is a value that changes per request inside the cached prefix.

c11.output:
no cache      $1,000.00
cached        $100.01
poisoned      $1,250.00  (every call a write)
saved         $899.99  (90.0%)
notice: These numbers are arithmetic from list prices, not a measurement: 5,000-token prefix, 100,000 calls, Sonnet 5.5 at $2 per million input tokens.
A poisoned cache costs 25% more than not caching at all, because every call pays the write premium and none gets the read discount.
The multipliers depend on the model: reads are 0.05x on Opus 5.5 and 0.025x on Fable 5.1, so rerun the cell with your model's numbers.

checkpoint.q: What is the prefix order? (three things, in order)
checkpoint.a: tools, then system, then messages. The cache key is built over that rendered order, so a change at any level invalidates that level and everything after it. That is why changing a tool definition breaks the system and message caches too.

checkpoint.q: Name three ways to invalidate a cache.
checkpoint.a: Any byte change before the breakpoint does it: a timestamp or request ID interpolated into the system prompt, adding, removing or reordering tool definitions, or non-deterministic JSON key order in serialized content. Switching models also misses, because caches are model-scoped, and changing thinking, effort or tool_choice invalidates the message-level cache. Finally, an entry simply expires if nothing reads it within its TTL.

checkpoint.q: Where do you place breakpoints, and why does content order matter?
checkpoint.a: Put a breakpoint at the end of the stable content, typically the last block of the static system prompt or the last tool, and keep everything volatile after it; you get at most four breakpoints per request. Order matters because the match is an exact prefix: stable content placed after a volatile value can never be reused, however many markers you add.
